english: I don't think I can make it today
usage: I don't think I can make it today
Polite; the soft, standard way to back out of plans
I don't think I can come today
I'm afraid I won't be able to attend today
Formal 합쇼체, to a boss or in a work message
오늘 참석 못 할 것 같아요
I don't think I can attend today
참석하다 ('attend') for a meeting/event rather than a casual hangout
examples: 미안한데 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
Sorry, but I don't think I can make it today.
Open with 미안한데 ('sorry, but') to cushion the bad news — bare 못 갈 것 같아요 without it can feel abrupt
저 오늘 좀 아파서 못 갈 것 같아요.
I'm a bit sick today, so I don't think I can come.
좀 아파서 ('a bit sick, so') gives a brief, face-saving reason before the cancellation
A: 오늘 회식 오시죠? / B: 죄송한데 오늘 못 갈 것 같습니다. 갑자기 일이 생겨서요.
A: You're coming to the team dinner tonight, right? / B: Sorry, I don't think I can make it — something came up.
Formal 같습니다 fits the work setting; 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 as a vague, face-saving reason
nuance: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 is 못 ('cannot') + 가다 ('to go') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), so literally 'it seems I can't go today.' The whole trick is the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge: Korean almost never uses a flat 못 가요 to cancel, because that sounds blunt and final, almost like a refusal. Wrapping it in 같아요 softens it into a gentle 'I don't think I can make it' — even when you are 100% certain you can't go, you still say 같아요. The nearest near-synonym 안 갈 것 같아요 uses 안 ('won't, by choice') instead of 못 ('can't, prevented'), and that difference matters: 못 implies an external barrier (work, illness), which reads as a valid excuse, while 안 implies you simply choose not to come — so for canceling, default to 못. Common collocations: 미안한데/죄송한데 + 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 (opener + cancellation), and a trailing reason like 일이 생겨서요. Register: 같아요 for everyday polite, 같습니다 for work/superiors, 같아 for close friends only. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'I can't make it' word-for-word and dropping the hedge, producing a cold 오늘 못 가요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it seems I cannot go today' — the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge is the key: even when you are certain you can't come, Korean social norms call for this softened prediction form. A flat 못 가요 would sound like a sharp refusal, not an apologetic cancellation.

Use this when canceling any plan — casual meetup, work dinner, appointment — at any point from hours before to the day of. 같아요 is standard polite (친구의 친구, 직장 동료); 같습니다 for a boss or formal work chat; 같아 only among close friends. Always open with 미안한데/죄송한데 before the cancellation line.

안 갈 것 같아요 ('I don't think I'll go') uses 안 (volitional 'won't') not 못 (inability 'can't'). 못 sounds like circumstances stopped you; 안 sounds like you just don't feel like it — so for a polite cancellation, 못 갈 것 같아요 is always safer.

Add a reason before: 일이 생겨서 못 갈 것 같아요. Substitute the destination: 오늘 못 올 것 같아요 ('I don't think I can come', if the other person is the host). For leaving early: 먼저 나가야 할 것 같아요 ('I think I have to head out first').
Dropping the hedge and saying 오늘 못 가요 reads as blunt and cold in Korean. Always wrap it: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요. Also, never render 'make it' as 만들다 — 만들다 means 'create/build'; use the motion verb 가다/오다.

mistakes: Saying a flat 오늘 못 가요 to cancel.
Without the hedge it sounds blunt and final, almost like a refusal. Soften it to 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 — the -ㄹ 것 같다 makes it polite and apologetic even when you're certain.
Using 안 갈 것 같아요 when something is preventing you.
안 = 'won't (by choice)', which can sound like you just don't feel like coming. If circumstances stop you, use 못 ('can't'): 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
Mistranslating 'make it' literally with 만들다.
'Make it' here is idiomatic English for 'attend'. 만들다 means 'to build/create' — never 오늘 못 만들어요. Use 못 가요/못 갈 것 같아요.

usage: Polite; the all-purpose vague reason for canceling
반말 / trailing reason, to a friend
An urgent matter suddenly came up
Add 급한 ('urgent') to stress it's serious and unavoidable
집에 ('at home') hints at a family matter without details
examples: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요. 다음에 봬요.
Something came up, so… Let's meet next time.
Trailing -서요 lets the excuse stand alone; the unsaid conclusion is 'so I can't come' — Korean listeners fill it in politely
미안, 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 못 갈 것 같아.
Sorry, something came up so I don't think I can come today.
반말 to a friend, chaining the reason into the full cancellation line
A: 오늘 왜 못 와요? / B: 죄송합니다, 갑자기 급한 일이 생겨서 오늘 미팅 참석이 어려울 것 같습니다.
A: Why can't you come today? / B: I'm sorry — an urgent matter suddenly came up, so I don't think I can attend today's meeting.
Formal work register: 급한 일 + 참석이 어렵다, responding directly to a 'why' question
nuance: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 is 갑자기 ('suddenly') + 일 ('a matter/thing/work') + 생기다 ('to arise/come up') + -어서 ('because') + 요 (polite ender). This is the socially perfect vague excuse: 일 is deliberately broad — it can mean work, an errand, a family thing, anything — so you can bow out without disclosing private details, and Koreans accept it without prying. The trailing -서요 (reason + 요, with the main clause left unsaid) is extremely natural; it implies '…so I can't make it' without you having to spell out the blunt part. The nearest near-synonym 바빠서요 ('because I'm busy') is fine but can sound like a weaker brush-off since busyness feels self-inflicted; 일이 생겨서요 implies a concrete unforeseen event and lands as stronger, more legitimate. The 갑자기 ('suddenly') is what signals this wasn't your fault — it's the difference between a genuine emergency and a vague excuse, so keep it. Watch the verb: it must be 생기다 ('to arise', intransitive) with subject particle 이/가; learners wrongly use 만들다 or the wrong particle 을/를.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'because a thing suddenly arose'. The power is in what it does NOT say: 일 is kept vague on purpose, and the trailing -서요 leaves the consequence ('so I can't come') unsaid. Koreans read the full meaning without it being spoken — this is intentional, face-saving indirectness.

Works in almost any cancellation context: casual hangout, work meeting, family dinner. The trailing -서요 is the polite everyday register; for work/superiors use 갑자기 급한 일이 생겨서 참석이 어렵게 되었습니다. In 반말 the 요 drops: 갑자기 일이 생겨서.

바빠서요 ('because I'm busy') feels weaker — busyness can look like poor planning. 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 signals an unforeseeable event, so it carries more social legitimacy. 급한 일이 생겨서요 is even stronger, implying genuine urgency.

Specifying the domain: 집에 일이 생겨서요 (family matter), 회사에 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 (work issue). Stacking with the cancel: 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요. More formal: 갑작스럽게 일이 생겨서요 (갑작스럽다 = 'abrupt/sudden', more written register).

Two particle/verb traps in one phrase: (1) 생기다 is intransitive — the subject is 일이, never 일을. (2) Never use 만들다 ('make/create') here: 일을 만들었어요 means 'I caused trouble', not 'something came up'. The event arises on its own; you don't make it.

mistakes: Saying 일을 만들었어요 to mean 'something came up'.
만들다 ('make') + 일을 means 'I created work/trouble'. The event-arising verb is 생기다, used with 이: 일이 생겼어요 / 일이 생겨서요.
Wrong particle: 일을 생겨서요.
생기다 is intransitive and takes the subject particle: 일이 생겨서요, not 일을. The thing 'arises' on its own; you don't act on it.
Over-explaining the private reason.
The point of 일이 생겨서요 is its vagueness — Koreans won't pry. Volunteering every detail can sound like over-justifying; the trailing -서요 is enough.

english: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
usage: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
Is it okay if I cancel?
Would it be alright to cancel?
괜찮을까요 ('would it be alright') is a touch gentler
Would it be a problem if I canceled today?
examples: 미안한데 오늘 약속 취소해도 될까요?
Sorry, but would it be okay to cancel today's plans?
미안한데 softens the request before asking permission — opening with the apology first is the Korean norm
나 컨디션이 너무 안 좋은데 약속 취소해도 돼?
I'm really not feeling well — is it okay if I cancel?
반말 with 컨디션이 안 좋다 ('feeling off') as the reason; 취소해도 돼? stays light and direct between friends
A: 내일 만나기로 했잖아요. / B: 정말 죄송한데 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 약속 취소하면 안 될까요?
A: We were supposed to meet tomorrow. / B: I'm really sorry, but something came up — would it be a problem if I canceled today?
The 안 될까요 negative form is the most apologetic variant; use it when you feel especially bad
nuance: 약속 취소해도 될까요? is 약속 ('plans/appointment/promise') + 취소하다 ('to cancel', Sino-Korean 取消) + -아도 되다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder, may I?'). Framing the cancellation as a permission question is the polite, face-saving move: instead of announcing you ARE canceling, you ask whether you may, handing the other person dignity. Note 약속 carries real weight — it covers plans to meet, an appointment, AND a promise, so canceling 약속 carries a slight sense of breaking your word, which is exactly why you ask so gently. The near-synonym 약속 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel our plans', -ㄹ게요) just DECLARES the cancellation and can feel one-sided/abrupt for personal plans; reserve 취소할게요 for impersonal bookings (a restaurant reservation, a delivery). The negative-question variant 취소하면 안 될까요? ('would it be a problem if I canceled?') sounds even more apologetic — handy when you feel genuinely bad. The direct English-speaker trap is saying 약속을 깨다 ('break the appointment') — 깨다 literally 'shatters' a promise and sounds like a betrayal; use 취소하다 for an ordinary cancel.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I cancel the plans, would it be okay?'. The -아도 되다 framing is crucial: you are ASKING permission to cancel, not announcing it. This turns a potentially hurtful action into a considerate request, preserving the other person's face.

Use with anyone you have made personal plans with — a friend, a colleague, a date. 될까요 is standard polite; 괜찮을까요 is slightly warmer and more apologetic (better when you feel extra bad); 돼? is the 반말 version for close friends only. Never use 깨도 될까요 (깨다= shatter) for a normal cancel.

약속 취소할게요 (-ㄹ게요) declares YOUR decision unilaterally — appropriate for impersonal bookings (식당 예약 취소할게요 'I'll cancel the restaurant reservation'). For plans with a person, asking with 될까요? is more considerate. 약속을 깨다 ('break a promise') is too harsh for an ordinary cancellation.

약속 전체를 취소할게요 (direct declaration, for impersonal bookings); 오늘 약속 취소해도 될까요? (asking for today); 이번 약속은 취소하고 다음에 다시 잡을까요? ('shall we cancel this one and reschedule?'). For escalating apology: 정말 죄송한데 약속 취소해도 괜찮을까요? Switching cancel to reschedule: 취소 말고 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? ('instead of canceling, could we move it to another day?'). 취소하다 also pairs with 예약 (reservation): 식당 예약 취소할게요 — but for personal plans always use the permission-question form.

(1) Saying 약속을 깨도 될까요? — 깨다 ('shatter/break') sounds like betraying a serious vow; use 취소하다 for a normal cancel. (2) Treating 약속 as only 'a promise' and reaching for 계획 ('plan') instead — 약속 is exactly the right word for 'our plans to meet'.

mistakes: Saying 약속을 깨도 될까요? to cancel plans.
깨다 ('break/shatter') sounds like betraying a serious promise. For ordinary plans use 취소하다: 약속 취소해도 될까요?
Declaring 약속 취소할게요 to a person.
-ㄹ게요 announces your decision and can feel abrupt for plans involving someone else. Ask permission instead: 취소해도 될까요? Save 취소할게요 for bookings/reservations.
Confusing 약속 with only 'a promise'.
약속 also means 'plans/an appointment to meet'. 'Cancel our plans' is 약속 취소하다 — it's the correct everyday word, not just for breaking a vow.

english: Could we change the time of our plans?
usage: Could we change our meeting time?
Polite; asking to move the time, not cancel
변경하다 (Sino-Korean) sounds more formal/official than 바꾸다
Could we push the time back just a little?
미루다 ('postpone') when you want it slightly later, not a different slot
examples: 혹시 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요?
Could we possibly change our meeting time?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens the request — a key politeness opener before any favor
나 길이 막혀서 그런데 약속 시간 30분만 늦춰도 돼?
I'm stuck in traffic — can we push it 30 minutes later?
30분만 늦추다 ('push back just 30 min') is more precise than 바꾸다 when you know the direction and amount
A: 오늘 3시에 만나기로 했는데요. / B: 죄송한데 회의 시간 좀 변경해도 될까요? 오전은 일정이 꽉 차서요.
A: We agreed on 3 o'clock today. / B: Sorry, could we change the meeting time? My morning is fully booked.
변경하다 + reason 일정이 꽉 차다 ('schedule is packed') fits a professional exchange
nuance: 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is 약속 시간 ('meeting time') + 좀 (softener) + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). The crucial distinction from the cancel card: this CHANGES the time but KEEPS the plan, whereas 취소 kills it — and Koreans much prefer rescheduling to canceling, so this is the friendlier ask. 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for changing/swapping; the Sino-Korean 변경하다 means the same but is more formal (business emails, official bookings). If you specifically want it LATER, the precise verb is 미루다 or 늦추다 ('postpone/push back'); if EARLIER, 당기다 ('move up, pull forward'). To swap one specific time for another, the pattern is A를 B로 바꾸다 — the 를 on the original slot and 로 on the new one are both required. The 좀 here is a politeness softener, not 'a little'; add 조금만 for a small shift. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping the -로 on the new time: say 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요?, not 3시를 5시 바꿔도 될까요?. (2) Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend — sounds overly stiff; stick with 바꾸다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I change the meeting time a bit, would it be okay?' — the -아도 될까요 again frames the change as a permission request, not a declaration. This is the socially preferred move: rescheduling rather than canceling, and asking rather than announcing.

Use when you need to adjust the clock time while keeping the same day and same meeting. 될까요? is standard polite; 변경해도 될까요? is more formal (work context); 바꿔도 돼? is 반말 between friends. For a superior, upgrade to 변경해도 괜찮으실까요?.

바꾸다 = everyday 'change/swap' (casual to semi-formal). 변경하다 = Sino-Korean 'modify/revise' (formal, documents, official contexts). 미루다/늦추다 = specifically 'push LATER'. 당기다/앞당기다 = specifically 'move EARLIER'. If you know the direction, the directional verb is more natural than the neutral 바꾸다.
Slot-swap pattern: 3시를 5시로 바꾸다 ('change 3 to 5'). Directional variants: 시간을 좀 미루다 (later) / 시간을 좀 당기다 (earlier). Honorific escalation: 시간 변경해도 괜찮으실까요? for a senior.

(1) Dropping -로 when swapping slots: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? — both particles (를 on old, 로 on new) are required. (2) Reaching for 변경하다 with friends — it sounds too formal; use 바꾸다 in casual conversation. (3) 시간을 옮기다 ('move/relocate') works for dates and venues but is less idiomatic for a clock time; prefer 바꾸다 or 늦추다/당기다.

mistakes: Forgetting -로 when swapping times: 3시를 5시 바꿔도 돼요?
To replace A with B you mark the new value with -로: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? ('change 3 to 5'). Without -로 it's incomplete.
Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend.
변경하다 is Sino-Korean and sounds official/business-like. With friends use the everyday 바꾸다: 시간 좀 바꿔도 돼?
Saying 시간을 옮기다 for the clock time.
옮기다 ('move/relocate') fits dates or venues (날짜를 옮기다) better than the time of day. For the time, prefer 바꾸다 or, for 'later', 미루다/늦추다.

english: Could we push it to another day?
usage: Could we move it to another day?
Polite; asks to postpone to a different day
Can we do it another day?
Would it be possible to push it to another day?
-ㄹ 수 있을까요 ('would it be possible') is a touch softer/formal
Could we move it to next week?
Swap in a concrete time (다음 주 'next week') instead of vague 다른 날
examples: 오늘은 좀 힘들 것 같은데, 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요?
Today's a bit hard — could we move it to another day?
오늘은 힘들 것 같다 is a gentle 'today doesn't work' that sets up the postpone request without blaming anyone
미안, 나 이번 주 너무 바빠서 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼?
Sorry, I'm so busy this week — can we do it another day?
반말 with a busy-week reason; 이번 주 ('this week') makes the constraint concrete
A: 이번 주 금요일은 어때요? / B: 죄송한데 다음 주로 미룰 수 있을까요? 그때는 꼭 시간 낼게요.
A: How about this Friday? / B: Sorry, could we push it to next week? I'll definitely make time then.
꼭 시간 낼게요 ('I'll be sure to make time') shows good faith and keeps the door open
nuance: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? is 다른 날 ('another day') + -로 (direction particle 'to') + 미루다 ('to postpone/put off') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). 미루다 is THE everyday verb for postponing — pushing an event to a later point — and the -로 on 다른 날 is essential: you move it TO another day (다른 날로, 다음 주로, 주말로); dropping -로 sounds off. Two key contrasts: (1) 미루다 vs. 취소하다 — 미루다 keeps the plan alive for later (much preferred socially), 취소하다 kills it; reach for 미루다 whenever you can still meet, just not now. (2) 미루다 vs. 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期) — both mean 'postpone', but 연기하다 is formal/official (postponing an event, a wedding, a match: 경기가 연기됐다); for casual plans use 미루다. Be aware 미루다 also means 'to procrastinate' (일을 자꾸 미루다), but paired with 다른 날로 it unambiguously means 'reschedule to another day'. The English-speaker trap is confusing 미루다 ('postpone in time') with 밀다 ('push physically').

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I push it to another day, would it be okay?' The verb 미루다 carries the core idea of deferring to a later time. It is a more cooperative, relationship-preserving move than 취소하다 — you're not dropping the plan, you're keeping it alive.

Use when you can't make a specific day but genuinely want to meet another time. 될까요? is standard polite. 돼? is 반말. For extra deference: 다른 날로 미룰 수 있을까요? (-ㄹ 수 있을까요 is more tentative). In formal work contexts: 일정을 연기해도 괜찮겠습니까?.

미루다 (casual/everyday) vs. 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期, formal/official): 약속을 미루다 for personal plans; 행사/경기를 연기하다 for public events. 취소하다 ends the plan; 미루다 saves it. These three verbs form a natural set for any learner studying rescheduling.
Replace 다른 날 with a specific target: 다음 주로 미루다, 주말로 미루다, 다음 달로 미루다. Softer: 조금 미뤄도 될까요? ('could we push it back a bit?'). Formal: 일정을 연기해도 될까요?

(1) Dropping -로: 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요? — the destination requires -로 because you are moving the event TO that day. (2) Confusing 미루다 ('postpone in time') with 밀다 ('push physically'): 약속을 밀다 is not idiomatic — say 약속을 미루다. (3) Over-using 연기하다 in casual conversation — it sounds stiff and bureaucratic between friends; 미루다 is the natural word.

mistakes: Dropping -로: 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요?
You postpone something TO a day, so the target takes -로: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? Without -로 the destination is unmarked and sounds incomplete.
Using 연기하다 for casual plans with a friend.
연기하다 is formal/official ('postpone an event'). For everyday plans say 미루다: 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼? Save 연기되다 for matches/ceremonies.
Confusing 미루다 with 밀다.
밀다 is 'to push (physically)' or 'to shove'. 'Postpone' is 미루다. 약속을 밀다 isn't the idiom — say 약속을 미루다 / 다른 날로 미루다.

usage: 뵙다 (humble 'see') to an elder/superior; very respectful
Let's see each other again sometime
또 ('again') warms it up, keeps the door open
examples: 오늘은 아쉽지만 다음에 봬요.
It's a shame about today, but let's meet another time.
아쉽지만 ('it's a pity, but') keeps the tone warm rather than dismissive — the combination signals genuine regret
알겠어, 그럼 다음에 봐!
Got it, see you next time then!
반말 reply accepting a reschedule; 그럼 ('well then') bridges the acceptance naturally
A: 오늘 정말 죄송했습니다. / B: 괜찮아요. 다음에 꼭 뵐게요.
A: I'm really sorry about today. / B: It's okay. I'll be sure to see you next time.
The humble 뵐게요 (from 뵙다) is appropriate when speaking to or about a senior; 꼭 ('definitely') makes the promise feel sincere
nuance: 다음에 봬요 is 다음에 ('next time / another time') + 봬요, the contracted polite form of 뵈어요 (from 뵙다, the humble verb 'to see/meet someone'). This is the gentle closer that softens a cancellation — by promising a future meeting, it signals 'no hard feelings, we'll still get together.' Spelling is a notorious trap: 봬요 (= 뵈어요) is correct, NOT 뵈요; in speech both sound like 'bwae-yo', but 뵈요 is a misspelling even many native speakers make. Register matters here: 뵙다 is the humble/honorific verb for 'see/meet', so 봬요 and 뵐게요 carry extra warmth and respect — more polite than plain 봐요/볼게요 (from 보다, the neutral 'see'). To an elder, boss, or someone you respect, 다음에 뵐게요 is gracious; among peers 다음에 봬요 is fine; for close friends 다음에 봐 is natural. The near-synonym 다음에 만나요 (from 만나다 'to meet') is also correct and slightly more direct, but 봬요 carries that built-in humble warmth. English-speaker pitfall: treating 다음에 as a firm commitment — it's an intentionally vague 'sometime', not a scheduled meeting. To actually pin down a next date, add 다음에 언제 볼까요?.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'next time, (let me) see you (humbly)'. The humble verb 뵙다 makes even a parting phrase carry a nuance of respect — you are positioning yourself below the other person. It turns a simple 'see you later' into something genuinely warm and considerate.

Said at the end of a cancellation, as a text sign-off, or when parting after a meeting cut short. 봬요 is standard polite (적당한 격식); 뵐게요 adds your own volition and is more forward-looking ('I will see you'); 봐 is 반말. With superiors: 꼭 다음에 뵐게요 is the ideal close after any cancellation.

다음에 만나요 (from 만나다) is natural and slightly more neutral — it doesn't carry the humble register of 뵙다 and works well among equals. 다음에 봬요 is slightly warmer because of the humble verb. Both can follow a cancellation; choose by your relationship.

다음에 또 봬요 ('see you again sometime') — 또 warms it up. 다음에 꼭 봬요 ('let's definitely meet next time') — 꼭 makes it a mild promise. 그때 봬요 ('see you then') — when a next date has already been set. To fix a real meeting: 다음에 언제 볼까요?

(1) Misspelling/saying 뵈요 instead of 봬요 — 봬요 is the contraction of 뵈어요; 뵈요 is simply wrong. Think of it like 돼요 (= 되어요): the ㅓ from 어 contracts in. (2) Pinning a date to 다음에 — it's a warm but vague 'sometime'; if you mean a real next meeting, say 다음에 언제 볼까요?.

mistakes: Writing or saying 뵈요 instead of 봬요.
봬요 is the contraction of 뵈어요; 뵈요 is a misspelling. When in doubt, expand it: 뵈어요 → 봬요. (Same logic as 돼요 from 되어요.)
Using plain 봐요 to an elder/superior.
보다's plain 봐요 is fine among peers, but for respect use the humble 뵙다: 다음에 뵐게요/봬요 lowers yourself politely before them.
Reading 다음에 as a firm commitment.
다음에 봬요 is a warm, vague 'sometime'. It doesn't fix a date. To actually schedule, follow up with 언제 볼까요? or 날짜 정해요.

english: I think I'll be a little late
usage: I think I'll be a little late
Polite; heads-up that you're running behind
I'm afraid I'll be a little late
Formal 합쇼체, to a boss / in a work chat
Give a number (10분 정도) so they can plan
examples: 미안, 나 조금 늦을 것 같아. 5분만 기다려 줘.
Sorry, I think I'll be a bit late. Give me 5 minutes.
반말 + 기다려 줘 ('please wait for me') — text this the moment you know, not after you've already arrived late
길이 막혀서 한 10분 늦을 것 같아요. 먼저 들어가 계세요.
Traffic's bad, so I'll be about 10 minutes late. Please go on in first.
먼저 들어가 계세요 ('go in ahead') is the considerate add-on that shows you respect the other person's time
A: 지금 어디예요? / B: 죄송합니다, 차가 너무 막혀서 15분 정도 늦을 것 같습니다.
A: Where are you now? / B: I'm sorry, traffic is terrible, so I'll be about 15 minutes late.
Formal register with a concrete delay; responding directly to 'where are you?' with an ETA is natural
nuance: 조금 늦을 것 같아요 is 조금 ('a little') + 늦다 ('to be late') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('I think / it seems'). This isn't a cancel — it's the polite running-late heads-up, and in Korea sending it the moment you know you'll be late is basic courtesy; silently arriving late is read as inconsiderate. The -ㄹ 것 같다 functions as a genuine prediction here, not just politeness softening, so 같아요 is doubly natural. The verb 늦다 is an adjective-verb ('to be late') and must not be confused with 늦추다 ('to delay/push back something', transitive): you 늦추다 a schedule, but you yourself 늦다. Pair with a specific number (10분/15분 정도) and a reason (길이 막혀서 'because of traffic') to show consideration. The near-synonym 늦어요 (flat 'I'm late') sounds after-the-fact and less apologetic; 늦을 것 같아요 is a proactive forward-looking warning. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) confusing 늦다 ('late in time') with 느리다 ('slow in speed') — 'I'll be late' is 늦다, not 느려요. (2) Translating 'I'll be late' as 저는 늦을 것입니다 — accurate but stilted; 늦을 것 같아요 is the natural spoken form.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it seems I will be a little late'. Unlike the cancellation cards where -ㄹ 것 같다 is mainly a politeness hedge, here it is also a genuine prediction — you're informing someone of an expected delay. Both uses coexist, making 같아요 the only natural choice for this sentence.

Send this as a text the moment you realize you'll be late — not after you arrive. 같아요 is standard polite; 같습니다 for work; 같아 for close friends. Adding a specific delay (10분 정도) and a reason (길이 막혀서) is courteous and reduces the other person's anxiety. Follow with 먼저 들어가 계세요 ('go on in') or 기다려 줘 ('wait for me') depending on the situation.

늦어요 ('I'm late') is a flat present-tense statement — better for when you're already on-site and apologizing. 늦을 것 같아요 is proactive: you're warning before it happens. The proactive form is always more considerate.

Add amount: 10분 늦을 것 같아요. Add reason: 길이 막혀서 / 버스가 늦어서 ('the bus is running late'). Add ETA follow-through: 늦을 것 같은데, 5시쯤 도착할 것 같아요 ('I'll be late — I think I'll arrive around 5'). For leaving early from an ongoing event: 먼저 일어나야 할 것 같아요.

(1) Confusing 늦다 ('late in time') with 느리다 ('slow in speed'): 'I'll be late' = 늦을 것 같아요, never 느릴 것 같아요. (2) Confusing 늦다 (be late, intransitive) with 늦추다 ('to delay/push back something', transitive): 'I will be late' = 늦을 것 같아요; 'let's push the meeting back' = 회의를 늦추다. Do not say 저를 늦출 것 같아요.

mistakes: Saying 늦출 것 같아요 to mean 'I'll be late'.
늦추다 is transitive ('delay something', e.g. a meeting). For your own lateness use the adjective 늦다: 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
Confusing 늦다 with 느리다.
느리다 = 'slow (in speed)'; 늦다 = 'late (in time)'. 'I'll be late' is 늦을 것 같아요, not 느릴 것 같아요.
Just showing up late with no message.
In Korea a proactive heads-up is expected courtesy. Text 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (ideally with minutes + reason) as soon as you know, rather than arriving silently late.
